prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading all eight round-1 files I keep B057 to Katori and Ye as a single-part prize, and my confidence is higher than in round 1 because seven members, several of whom moved from a different opening first choice, reached it through independent scientific reasoning rather than through counting. The criterion I take from the will, and which I stated in public as a discovery or invention with identifiable originators, is met here: magic-wavelength trapping is one bounded idea with a named originator, and its consequence, fractional uncertainty near 1e-18 reproduced in many laboratories, is a measured result and not a promise. The credit is two people, Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking strontium lattice clocks to record accuracy and stability, and I have found no documented contribution that would force a third name. I would draft the citation around trapping of neutral atoms in an optical lattice at the magic wavelength, and not around optical clocks or frequency standards generally, which answers the chair's first question about separating this from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot dispose of entirely is that this is precision metrology standing on two recent prizes. A sceptical reader can say the lattice clock is a superb refinement and that the comparison technology belongs to Hall and Hansch, while ion clocks reached comparable accuracy in parallel. I think a tightly worded citation answers the novelty objection, but it does not remove the fact that the line is less sharp than for a new phenomenon. Other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto) are outside the credit, and a two-name prize necessarily leaves them out; I accept that as the normal cost of the three-person limit and not a reason to widen the credit. Finally, I have to be honest that my own opening first choice, B048, found no support, and I have weighed the colleagues' reasons for that on their merits and not as a reflection of my field.

responses.point: Mehlig says that aberration-corrected electron microscopy mainly enables materials science and chemistry rather than physical understanding, whereas the lattice clock changes which physical questions can be asked, such as gravitational redshift and constants variation on laboratory scales.
responses.response: This is a fair criticism and I have moved on it. From inside microscopy I can say the corrector has changed physics as well, for example atomic-resolution imaging of oxide interfaces and defects, but I cannot honestly claim that it tests fundamental physics the way a 1e-18 clock does. The invention criterion is satisfied for B048, but when the committee must pick one achievement for this year, the case that makes new measurements of nature possible is stronger, and I no longer prefer B048 first.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B053 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a new organising principle for band insulators and a mature theory-plus-experiment case, while accepting B057 as a good outcome, and he raises the Hasan versus Mele choice and the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit.
responses.response: I take B053 seriously and keep it as my first alternative: the Z2 classification is genuinely new and the field is mature. My difficulty is attribution and not worth. The experimental quantum spin Hall observation rests on a theory prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) that sits outside his three names, the three-dimensional materials add Fu and Hasan, and the 2016 prize covers neighbouring topological ground. A three-name credit would therefore have to exclude people whose contributions the community considers essential, while the B057 credit is essentially uncontested. I would support B053 only if B057 were set aside and the citation could be drawn so narrowly that those omissions are defensible, and I am not yet convinced that it can.

responses.point: Kroll flags his research stay in John Hall's laboratory, documents no tie to Katori or Ye, and leaves the question of recusal on B057 to the chair, while arguing that the achievement is complete whether or not the second is redefined.
responses.response: I would not ask for recusal. A stay in the laboratory of someone honoured for the comb in 2005 is a disclosure the record should carry, but it is not a tie to either proposed laureate, and Kroll's spectroscopy expertise is exactly what the committee needs to judge the claims about stability. I also agree with his view on timing: the scientific achievement, the 1e-18 performance and its reproduction, is complete, and the redefinition of the second is a later metrological decision by a different body. I would not make it a condition.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, keeps B054 (IceCube) as a first alternative on the grounds that a new observational window may be a larger open question than metrological precision, and says that other lattice-clock contributors may need acknowledgement in the citation wording.
responses.response: I agree that the citation wording should be tight and I accept his framing of B054 as a fair alternative if the committee prefers a new window on nature. Where I stay with B057 is on maturity and attribution: the diffuse flux is secure but source associations are few and moderate, and it is unclear how three names can be separated from the collaboration and from AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND. On acknowledging other lattice groups, I would handle that in the committee's popular and scientific background text, not by adding names to the prize.

responses.point: Lindroth, who works in atomic physics, would accept B048 as a second part but says the clock has had the larger effect on fundamental physics, and she asks whether the citation wording can resolve credit for other clock groups.
responses.response: Her view of the relative weight is persuasive and, since she is the member closest to the physics of the clock, I give it extra weight. I am no longer proposing B048 as a second part: a two-part prize would also require a third and fourth name, and the three-person limit would then force exactly the credit compromise (Krivanek, the STEM corrector) that I think would be unfair. B048 is better kept as a considered later candidate on its own.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can agree a citation that names magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and separates it from frequency combs (2005) and single-quantum-system control (2012); I think it can, but the wording will carry much of the weight.
Whether the lattice clock will be read as a distinct invention or as a continuation of two earlier prizes; I have not fully removed that doubt, but I judge the concept distinct.
Whether other lattice-clock groups outside Katori and Ye are adequately handled by background text and not credit.
Whether B048 can be properly credited within three names given that Krivanek's STEM-corrector work lies outside the supplied credits, which affects only a later year.
statement.conflict_note: My field of transmission electron microscopy is adjacent to B048, and I would recuse from any final decision on B048; since I no longer prefer it, this affects only an alternative. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited names on B057. Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, which I note as a connection but not a conflict for B057. I do not consider Kroll's Hall connection a reason for recusal on B057.
